analysis.one_liner: Taxes paper made without recycled content, starting at 3% and rising to 12%.
analysis.headline: A bill to tax paper products that lack recycled content, with 69 bipartisan sponsors, was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and never received a hearing, vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put an excise tax on paper and paper products sold by manufacturers, producers, or importers that do not meet minimum recycled-content standards set by the EPA. The tax would start at 3% of the wholesale price in 1991 and climb one percentage point each year to 12% in 2000 and after. The goal is to make recycled paper cheaper relative to virgin paper, pushing manufacturers to use recovered materials and reducing the waste that ends up in landfills.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people would benefit from less paper waste going to landfills and from manufacturers shifting toward recycled materials, which the tax makes financially necessary. Recycling operations and collectors of recovered paper would see growing demand for their materials.

how_it_helps.text: The bill imposes an excise tax of 3% on wholesale sales of paper products without minimum recycled content, rising one percentage point per year to 12% in 2000 and after, so using recovered materials becomes cheaper than paying the tax [S2][S3].

It directs the EPA Administrator to issue guidelines, by the end of 1990, setting minimum recovered-material content standards for all paper and paper products not already covered by existing guidelines under the Solid Waste Disposal Act [S2][S3].
By steering manufacturers toward recovered materials, the tax would reduce the volume of paper landfilled or burned, a cost that falls on municipalities and residents [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Paper manufacturers, producers, and importers would owe the tax on non-recycled products, and they would pass part of the cost to businesses and consumers who buy paper that lacks recycled content. Producers would also face the expense of retooling to meet recycled-content standards.

drawbacks.text: The tax is passed through to prices, so consumers and businesses buying paper would pay more for products that do not meet recycled-content standards [S3].

The bill relies on EPA guidelines that did not yet exist — it required the agency to write recycled-content standards for most paper products by the end of 1990 — so the tax's reach and the costs of compliance were undefined when the bill was proposed [S3].
An excise tax hits all non-compliant paper equally, including sales to schools, governments, and small businesses, without exemptions for buyers who cannot switch to recycled stock [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is a straightforward economic nudge: make non-recycled paper progressively more expensive until manufacturers find recycled content cheaper. Consumers would pay somewhat higher prices in the short run, but the escalating rate gives the industry a decade to adjust, and the environmental gains — less landfill waste, more recycling — accrue broadly. The main weakness is that it delegates the key standards to future EPA guidelines, leaving businesses uncertain about what compliance would require.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee in April 1989, and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no vote, nothing — so it died when that Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Rep. Sam Gejdenson introduced the bill on April 5, 1989, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S1][S5].
Sixty-eight House members signed on as cosponsors — 60 Democrats and 8 Republicans — showing support across both parties [S4].
The action history shows no activity after the initial referral: the committee never scheduled a hearing or a vote, and the bill expired with the 101st Congress on January 3, 1991 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Paper manufacturers came out ahead: no tax was ever enacted on non-recycled paper, and they faced no new recycled-content mandate during this Congress. Communities gained nothing, since the incentives for recycling were never created.

for.name: Rep. Sam Gejdenson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it, proposing the escalating excise tax on non-recycled paper

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation, chaired by Rep. Dan Rostenkowski (D-IL)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it during the two years remaining in the Congress

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship crossed party lines — 60 Democrats and 8 Republicans signed on — and no floor vote ever split by party because the bill never left committee.

industries.note: The bill would tax their sales of non-recycled paper at rates climbing from 3% to 12%, giving them a strong financial reason to switch to recovered materials or pass the cost to customers. Its failure left them free to keep using virgin pulp with no tax penalty.
By penalizing paper made without recovered content, the bill would create guaranteed demand for collected waste paper. Its death meant no new market for recyclers was created.
